sections.title: Identification
sections.text: A small terrestrial fibrecap with a 2–4.5 cm cap, obtusely conical at first and later umbonate, ochre-yellow to rust-brown. The centre can have an olive-green tinge. Its dry, silky surface is usually smooth at the centre and finely radially fibrillose toward the margin. The gills start pale and become clay-brown, olive-brown or tobacco-brown. The pale stem is 2.5–7 cm tall and 2–6 mm wide; it may become partly green or blue-green, especially after handling or with age. The stem flesh may show the same tint. Spore print brown; spores smooth, ellipsoid to slightly almond-shaped, about 7–10 × 4–5 μm. The greenish tint may fade on drying and is not always visible.

sections.title: Habitat and ecology
sections.text: An ectomycorrhizal species reported on moist sandy soils, including deciduous plantations and wooded areas, often near poplar and willow roots; lime, oak and birch are also reported. European observations cited by Gartz are mainly from May and June, with fruiting sometimes continuing to October. Associated trees and sandy soil inform the ecology but cannot identify a specimen. The Dutch atlas notes that microscopy is required for a certain determination of Inocybe.

sections.title: Toxicology and caution
sections.text: Chemical analyses have confirmed psilocybin and baeocystin in this species; the alkaloid aeruginascin was also isolated and characterized from Inocybe aeruginascens. In one study by Gartz, muscarine was not detected in the 92 fruit bodies tested. That result applies to those samples and does not establish a general rule for every specimen or for the genus Inocybe, where muscarine is known in many other species. Accidental psychoactive poisonings have been reported. This is not a food mushroom: do not eat it, and do not use this entry to identify a collection. After ingestion, contact a poison centre or medical service immediately.

traits: Ochre to rust-brown cap, 2–4.5 cm wide, conical then umbonate, sometimes greenish at the centre
Gills pale at first, then clay-brown, olive-brown or tobacco-brown; brown spore print
Pale stem may develop a blue-green tint near the base or after handling; this colour can fade on drying
Ectomycorrhizal on moist sandy soils, often associated with poplar or willow
Psilocybin and baeocystin detected; muscarine was not detected in one study of 92 fruit bodies, limited to the samples tested
safetyNote: A psychoactive species with documented psilocybin and baeocystin. Muscarine was not detected in 92 fruit bodies in one study; this does not guarantee its absence from every specimen. Do not consume. After ingestion, contact a poison centre or emergency medical service immediately.
